what_it_does: Preserves formulas by helping prevent bacterial and yeast growth.
summary_short: Phenoxyethanol is a common cosmetic preservative used to keep products from spoiling. It is considered safe in cosmetics up to 1% and is described as a rare sensitizer, making it one of the better-tolerated preservative options.
summary_long:
Phenoxyethanol is used mainly as a preservative. It has broad antimicrobial activity, meaning it helps protect products against many bacteria and yeasts that could otherwise grow in water-based skincare, makeup, shampoo, and body-care formulas [PMID:unknown].

Its benefit is not to directly improve skin texture, acne, pigmentation, or aging signs. Instead, it helps keep a formula stable and safer to use over time by reducing microbial contamination risk. This is especially important in products that contain water or are repeatedly opened and exposed to air, fingers, or bathroom humidity.

The strongest cosmetic-specific safety review in the provided sources describes phenoxyethanol as safe for all consumers, including children, when used as a preservative at a maximum concentration of 1% [PMID:unknown]. Animal studies have reported systemic effects only at exposures far above normal cosmetic use, and the review describes phenoxyethanol as a rare sensitizer despite its widespread use.

For sensitive skin, phenoxyethanol is still worth noticing because any preservative can occasionally trigger irritation or allergy in susceptible people. Shampoo research also lists preservative systems among potential contact allergens in rinse-off products, although fragrance and certain surfactants are more commonly highlighted allergens [PMID:unknown]. If a product repeatedly stings, itches, or causes a rash, stopping use and checking the ingredient list can help identify a possible trigger.

Phenoxyethanol is often paired with other preservative boosters to broaden protection in finished formulas. There are no major skincare conflicts to avoid with common actives like niacinamide, retinoids, vitamin C, exfoliating acids, or sunscreen filters at normal cosmetic use levels.
quick_facts: Often used up to 1% in cosmetics
